extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulewriters, agency counsel, and members of the public who participate in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of the steps, legal requirements, and best practices for federal notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 553), including how to publish proposals, solicit and consider public comments, and publish final rules. Emphasizes procedural requirements, timing, public docketing, and optional engagement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies routinely issue rules to implement and interpret statutes, explain how they will exercise their discretion, and describe their procedures and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many rules are published in the Federal Register and the Code of Federal Regulations (see IIB-001). Understanding that rules can have substantive or interpretive effects helps determine applicable procedures and legal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation by publishing an NPRM in the Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency initiates the notice-and-comment rulemaking process by publishing a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM publication triggers the public participation period and is the formal starting point for APA notice-and-comment. Agencies commonly also notify the public via agency websites, social media, and other means (see ACUS Recs. 2013-5, 2011-8).

rubrics_metrics.name: NPRM content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM must describe the proposed rule, the legal authority for the rule, and opportunities for public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including clear descriptions of the proposed regulatory text, statutory authority, and how to comment ensures meaningful participation and helps satisfy procedural notice requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunity for public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must provide the public an opportunity to participate in the rulemaking through electronic or paper submission of written comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comment periods often last at least 30–60 days from publication of the NPRM (see ACUS Rec. 2011-2). Agencies may adopt additional engagement methods to solicit input (see ACUS Rec. 2018-7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public docketing of rulemaking materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies make comments, the NPRM, and supporting materials publicly available in an online docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining a publicly accessible docket (e.g., on Regulations.gov) supports transparency and allows commenters, courts, and stakeholders to review the administrative record (see ACUS Rec. 2013-4, IIB-005).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of relevant, timely-submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: After the comment period, the agency must consider all relevant, timely-submitted comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency's decisionmaking must reflect consideration of substantive timely comments; failure to consider significant, timely comments can expose the rule to legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop regulatory text and a preamble responding to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the agency decides to issue a final rule, it must develop the regulatory text along with a preamble explaining the rule’s basis and purpose and responding to all significant issues raised in the comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble should explain the factual and legal bases for the rule, describe changes made in response to comments, and answer significant objections to demonstrate reasoned decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of final rule and effective date requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency concludes the rulemaking by publishing the final rule and preamble in the Federal Register; the notice must specify the rule’s effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General timing: effective date must be at least 30 days after publication in the Federal Register; for 'major' rules, the Congressional Review Act requires at least 60 days after publication (5 U.S.C. § 801).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal law (the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 553) sets out the basic steps agencies must follow for notice-and-comment rulemaking and also describes several exceptions to that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must determine whether a particular rule falls within the APA’s notice-and-comment requirements or an exception (e.g., good cause) and follow the applicable procedure to avoid procedural challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with Executive orders and OMB/OIRA requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive orders and other Presidential directives also specify requirements for agency rulemaking, including for rules issued through notice-and-comment rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consult guidance from the Executive Office of the President (e.g., OIRA) and the ACUS Federal Administrative Procedure Sourcebook for interagency and executive-level requirements that supplement the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional: supplementing notice-and-comment with additional public engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies can supplement the basic notice-and-comment process as appropriate, for example by holding public meetings or soliciting public input before formally proposing a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS recommendations (Rec. 2020-1; Rec. 2018-7) discuss options for enhanced public engagement and early outreach; such practices can improve rule quality and stakeholder buy-in but do not replace APA procedural requirements.
